title: Acetylcholine Synthesis Support
pm_id: BRS1-FM2-PM6
mission: >-
  Maintain the capacity to form acetylcholine so cholinergic signalling for attention, working memory, and
  learning stays supplied.
parent_fm: BRS1(FM2)
parent_brs: BRS1
summary: >-
  Acetylcholine is made in nerve endings when choline is joined to acetyl-CoA, a cell-made acetate carrier.
  Diet can provide choline itself or choline from phosphatidylcholine, and vitamin B5 supports the acetyl-CoA
  side. Entry into the nerve ending still controls access to the reaction. The reaction supplies acetylcholine
  for later cholinergic signalling.

scientific_findings_intro: >-
  Transporter evidence identifies terminal choline uptake as a control step for acetylcholine synthesis, while
  human tracing demonstrates systemic assimilation of choline from dietary phosphatidylcholine.
  [[6]](#pm-ref-6) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Animal depletion and rescue studies support bounded pantothenate and
  one-carbon dependencies, with acetylcholine responses varying by experimental condition, region and age.
  [[8]](#pm-ref-8) [[9]](#pm-ref-9) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) The evidence therefore supports provision and local
  synthesis capacity without equating plasma choline delivery with neuronal release, attention benefit or a
  human dose response.
scientific_findings:
  - id: PM6-F1
    finding_label: High-affinity choline uptake controls substrate entry into cholinergic terminals
    finding_summary: >-
      The high-affinity choline transporter recovers choline into cholinergic nerve endings and is a major
      control point for acetylcholine production.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Substrate supply is not only a food-intake question: choline must reach the nerve terminal through a
      regulated transporter before choline acetyltransferase can use it.
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: >-
      Sodium-coupled high-affinity choline uptake through CHT/SLC5A7 is required to recover choline into
      cholinergic nerve terminals and commonly limits acetylcholine production under physiological demand.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      A focused transporter review shows that CHT recovers synaptic choline into cholinergic terminals, that
      inhibiting or genetically impairing this transport reduces cholinergic capacity, and that
      activity-dependent trafficking changes uptake capacity. This establishes terminal uptake as a control
      step upstream of the ChAT reaction.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      Transporter biology is largely mechanistic and preclinical. It does not show that ordinary choline
      intake changes CHT capacity in humans or that more dietary choline overcomes a transporter defect.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Ojiakor and Rylett (2020)
        citation_key: ojiakor_choline_transporter_2020
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ojiakor_choline_transporter_2020
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          CHT-mediated high-affinity choline uptake recovers choline into cholinergic terminals and is the
          principal regulated supply step for sustaining acetylcholine production.
        assessment:
          study: Review of CHT function, trafficking, genetic disruption, and pharmacological manipulation.
          population: Cellular, animal, human genetic, and neuropathology evidence; not a dietary trial.
          result: >-
            Reduced CHT function or availability limits choline uptake and cholinergic transmission, while
            neuronal activity recruits transport capacity.
          effect_magnitude: No pooled dietary effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Establishes the regulated choline-entry step required before acetylcholine synthesis.
          limitations: Does not test ordinary food intake or human brain synthesis after a meal.
      - label: Xue et al. (2024)
        citation_key: xue_human_cht1_structure_2024
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#xue_human_cht1_structure_2024
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        exposure_context: Controlled transport substrates and ions; not a dietary salt experiment.
        directional_finding: >-
          Human CHT1 structures and transport-site mutations identify sodium-dependent choline uptake;
          chloride binding has a distinct functional role.
        assessment:
          study: Human CHT1 cryo-EM structures and uptake/site-mutant experiments.
          population: Human transporter expressed in experimental systems.
          result: >-
            Human CHT1 structures and transport-site mutations identify sodium-dependent choline uptake;
            chloride binding has a distinct functional role.
          effect_magnitude: No additional magnitude inferred.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Human CHT1 structures and transport-site mutations identify sodium-dependent choline uptake;
            chloride binding has a distinct functional role.
          limitations: >-
            Transport-ion capacity does not establish that added dietary salt increases brain choline uptake
            or acetylcholine output. CNS homeostasis and membrane gradients intervene. Chloride is not assumed
            to have identical transport stoichiometry and is not independently admitted here.
          retrieval_scope: Primary structural and transport results retrieved 26 October 2026.
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Inazu (2019)
        citation_key: inazu_choline_transporters_2019
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#inazu_choline_transporters_2019
        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: >-
          Separates CTL1/CTL2-mediated choline handling at brain microvascular endothelium from CHT/SLC5A7
          uptake at cholinergic terminals.
        why_excluded: >-
          Does not test whether an oral choline exposure increases delivery to terminals or acetylcholine
          synthesis in humans.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F2
    finding_label: Choline and acetyl-CoA form acetylcholine via choline acetyltransferase
    finding_summary: >-
      Choline combines with acetyl-CoA through choline acetyltransferase to form acetylcholine. Necessity of
      those reactants is not proof that extra choline raises human brain acetylcholine.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Choline and acetyl-CoA are the two substrates. Phosphatidylcholine and pantothenate matter through
      provision routes assessed separately; vitamin B12 and folate do not act as ChAT cofactors.
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: >-
      Acetylcholine is formed from choline and acetyl-CoA by choline acetyltransferase; biochemical necessity
      is not intake-responsive human brain acetylcholine.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      A choline-acetyltransferase review and a modern choline-transporter review agree that ChAT transfers the
      acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to choline in cholinergic neurons. Together they establish the defining
      reaction and both substrates.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      Reaction and review evidence does not establish which substrate limits synthesis in every physiological
      state, an ordinary dietary dose response, or a human functional benefit.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Oda (1999)
        citation_key: oda_choline_1999
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#oda_choline_1999
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Choline acetyltransferase condenses choline and acetyl-CoA to form acetylcholine and is the defining
          synthetic enzyme in cholinergic neurons.
        assessment:
          study: Review of choline-acetyltransferase structure, distribution and pathology.
          population: Experimental and neuropathology literature; not a dietary sample.
          result: Identified choline and acetyl-CoA as the enzyme’s substrates.
          effect_magnitude: No dietary or clinical effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Establishes the acetylcholine-forming reaction.
          limitations: Enzyme and pathology review; not an intake-to-acetylcholine trial.
      - label: Ojiakor and Rylett (2020)
        citation_key: ojiakor_choline_transporter_2020
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ojiakor_choline_transporter_2020
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          ChAT transfers an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to choline in the neuronal cytoplasm after
          CHT-mediated choline entry.
        assessment:
          study: Review of CHT function and cholinergic terminal biology.
          population: Mechanistic, animal, and human genetic literature.
          result: Describes substrate entry followed by ChAT-dependent synthesis from choline and acetyl-CoA.
          effect_magnitude: No dietary effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Independently confirms the reaction participants within the presynaptic synthesis pathway.
          limitations: Does not measure human synthesis after dietary exposure.
    evidence_dependency:
      - >-
        Ojiakor and Rylett (2020) is also primary evidence in PM6-F1; reuse here establishes reaction
        placement after choline transport, not independent replication.
    connected_supportive_evidence:

        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: Reviews B-vitamin roles in brain energy and one-carbon chemistry.
        why_excluded: Does not establish vitamin B12 or folate as acetylcholine-synthesis cofactors.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F4
    finding_label: Dietary phosphatidylcholine is a choline-provision route
    finding_summary: >-
      Phosphatidylcholine is a choline-containing dietary form that is digested, absorbed, and remodelled. It
      provides choline but is not a second substrate in the ChAT reaction.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Represent phosphatidylcholine as Derived provision to choline, not as an independent
      acetylcholine-synthesis requirement.
    finding_statement: >-
      Dietary phosphatidylcholine is digested and remodelled into circulating phosphatidylcholine and free
      choline, establishing a dietary provision route to the direct choline substrate.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      In a randomized crossover tracer study in six healthy men, labelled phosphatidylcholine produced a
      delayed rise in labelled plasma choline and a larger phosphatidylcholine exposure than water-soluble
      choline forms. The tracer results directly establish digestion and systemic assimilation as a
      choline-containing dietary route.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      Small single-dose study in healthy men. Plasma appearance does not measure delivery to cholinergic
      terminals, acetylcholine synthesis, neurotransmitter release, attention, or clinical benefit.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Böckmann et al. (2023)
        citation_key: bockmann_choline_supplements_2023
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#bockmann_choline_supplements_2023
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: isolated-substance
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Oral labelled phosphatidylcholine produced delayed circulating labelled choline and the highest
          labelled phosphatidylcholine exposure among four tested choline forms.
        assessment:
          study: Randomized crossover stable-isotope comparison of four oral choline forms.
          population: Six healthy adult men.
          result: >-
            Phosphatidylcholine was digested and remodelled, with delayed plasma choline appearance and higher
            plasma phosphatidylcholine exposure.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            Delayed choline peak and approximately 2.3-fold higher peak labelled phosphatidylcholine than
            water-soluble forms.
          evidence_summary: Establishes phosphatidylcholine as an assimilated choline-provision route.
          limitations: Small sample; supplement bolus rather than whole food; no brain or acetylcholine measurement.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F5
    finding_label: Pantothenate supports the acetyl-CoA side of acetylcholine synthesis
    finding_summary: >-
      Pantothenate (vitamin B5) is needed to make coenzyme A, which cells use to form acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA
      supplies the acetyl group in acetylcholine.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Vitamin B5 is a biochemical precursor route to acetyl-CoA, not a ChAT cofactor or a second Direct
      Dietary Requirement. The evidence supports dependency and an animal depletion effect, not routine
      high-dose supplementation.
    finding_statement: >-
      Pantothenate supports acetylcholine-synthesis capacity through coenzyme A and acetyl-CoA formation, and
      severe chronic pantothenate depletion can reduce brain acetylcholine synthesis in rats.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      In rats exposed chronically to ethanol, brain pantothenate fell to 7% of control and labelled
      acetylcholine synthesis from pyruvate was inhibited; pantothenate co-administration raised brain
      pantothenate and acetylcholine synthesis. Together with the established acetyl-CoA reaction requirement,
      this closes the pantothenate → coenzyme A/acetyl-CoA → synthesis chain.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The intervention used chronic high-dose ethanol and pharmacological pantothenate doses in rats. It does
      not establish that ordinary B5 intake limits acetylcholine synthesis or that supplementation benefits
      adequately nourished humans.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Rivera-Calimlim et al. (1988)
        citation_key: rivera_calimlim_pantothenic_1988
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#rivera_calimlim_pantothenic_1988
        data_level: Preclinical
        exposure_context: isolated-substance
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Chronic ethanol depleted rat-brain pantothenate and inhibited acetylcholine synthesis, while
          pantothenate co-administration increased both brain pantothenate and synthesis.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Chronic and acute ethanol exposure with or without oral pantothenate in rats, measuring labelled
            acetylcholine synthesis.
          population: Rats; no human participants.
          result: >-
            The chronic four-month condition reduced brain pantothenate and acetylcholine synthesis;
            pantothenate co-treatment partly restored both.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            Brain pantothenate fell to 7% of control with chronic ethanol; synthesis differences were
            statistically significant but no transferable human effect size is available.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Directly links severe pantothenate depletion to reduced acetylcholine synthesis through acetyl-CoA
            provision.
          limitations: >-
            Ethanol-specific animal model, very high pantothenate doses, and no ordinary-diet or human
            outcome.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F6
    finding_label: One-carbon insufficiency can constrain the choline resource used for acetylcholine
    finding_summary: >-
      Folate- and B12-dependent one-carbon metabolism shares choline-related methyl resources. Dietary or
      genetic impairment can lower brain choline and acetylcholine in animal models.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      This supports a constrained-by mapping to the Methyl Donor Pool. It does not make folate, B12, or
      betaine ChAT cofactors or separate Direct Dietary Requirements.
    finding_statement: >-
      Inadequate folate-dependent or B12-dependent methionine-cycle capacity can disturb brain choline
      metabolism and lower acetylcholine availability, creating a supported shared-resource constraint on
      acetylcholine-synthesis capacity.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Dietary folate compromise lowered brain choline and acetylcholine in mice, with SAM restoring both under
      the deficient condition. Genetic methionine-synthase-reductase impairment likewise lowered hippocampal
      choline, betaine, and acetylcholine. A separate rat study found mixed, region- and age-dependent
      acetylcholine changes, showing that the effect is not uniform. Together these sources establish a
      shared-resource constraint while preserving biological variability.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      Animal dietary and genetic models measure metabolite pools more often than synthesis flux. They do not
      show that folate, B12, betaine, or SAM supplementation raises acetylcholine synthesis in
      nutrient-replete humans.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Chan et al. (2008)
        citation_key: chan_folate_acetylcholine_2008
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#chan_folate_acetylcholine_2008
        data_level: Preclinical
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Dietary folate compromise lowered mouse-brain choline and acetylcholine, while SAM supplementation
          under folate deficiency restored both pools.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Dietary folate deficiency across adult, aged, and genetically susceptible mouse models with SAM
            rescue.
          population: Mice of several genotypes and ages.
          result: >-
            Folate compromise reduced choline and acetylcholine; SAM restored these measures and cognitive
            performance in the deficient condition.
          effect_magnitude: Directionally consistent rescue across several mouse contexts; no human effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Supports the link from one-carbon donor insufficiency to loss of the choline resource used for
            acetylcholine.
          limitations: >-
            Mixed dietary, oxidative, age, and genotype contexts; pool concentrations rather than direct
            synthesis flux.
      - label: Jadavji et al. (2014)
        citation_key: jadavji_mtrr_choline_2014
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#jadavji_mtrr_choline_2014
        data_level: Preclinical
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Methionine-synthase-reductase-deficient mice had lower hippocampal choline, betaine, and
          acetylcholine with compensatory ChAT and AChE expression changes.
        assessment:
          study: Genetic mouse model of impaired methionine synthase reductase.
          population: Three-month-old wild-type and Mtrr-deficient mice.
          result: Deficiency reduced hippocampal choline, betaine, and acetylcholine and impaired short-term memory.
          effect_magnitude: Significant group differences reported; no dietary or human effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Adds B12-dependent methionine-cycle evidence to the shared-resource constraint.
          limitations: Genetic mouse model; altered concentration and enzyme expression do not quantify synthesis flux.
      - label: Crivello et al. (2010)
        citation_key: crivello_folate_choline_2010
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#crivello_folate_choline_2010
        data_level: Preclinical
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Ten weeks of folate deficiency changed brain acetylcholine in adult rats by region—lower in
          hippocampus but higher in cortex and striatum—with little brain effect in young rats.
        assessment:
          study: Controlled folate-deficient versus control diets in young and adult male rats.
          population: Male Sprague Dawley rats starting at four weeks or nine months.
          result: Brain choline and acetylcholine responses depended on age and region rather than moving uniformly.
          effect_magnitude: Significant regional differences; no whole-brain or human synthesis estimate.
          evidence_summary: Qualifies the constraint as context-dependent and prevents a universal lower-acetylcholine claim.
          limitations: Concentrations rather than synthesis flux; animal model; mixed regional direction.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F7
    finding_label: Acetyl-CoA supply is metabolically generated and compartmented
    finding_summary: >-
      Choline acetyltransferase works in the neuronal cytosol, while much acetyl-CoA is generated in
      mitochondria. Acetyl-unit transfer and local regeneration therefore form a separate substrate-supply
      control.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Acetyl-CoA availability can constrain synthesis, but this does not make glucose, pyruvate, citrate, or
      dietary acetyl-CoA separate Dietary Requirements for this PM.
    finding_statement: >-
      Cytosolic acetyl-CoA for acetylcholine synthesis is supplied through compartmented neuronal metabolism,
      and its availability can regulate synthesis independently of choline transport.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      A focused review of brain acetylcholine synthesis distinguishes mitochondrial acetyl-CoA production from
      the cytosolic ChAT reaction and reviews citrate cleavage, pyruvate-dependent production, and possible
      direct mitochondrial export routes. The evidence supports acetyl-CoA availability as a control point
      while leaving the proportional contribution of each route context-dependent.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The source literature is mechanistic and largely preclinical, and competing acetyl-unit transfer routes
      were not fully resolved. It does not establish glucose, pyruvate, citrate, or acetyl-CoA as useful
      dietary targets for this PM.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Jope (1979)
        citation_key: jope_choline_acetylcoa_1979
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#jope_choline_acetylcoa_1979
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Acetyl-CoA availability may limit acetylcholine synthesis, with evidence for citrate-lyase,
          pyruvate-dehydrogenase, and mitochondrial export routes supplying the cytosolic reaction.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Review of high-affinity choline transport, acetyl-CoA production, compartmentation, and regulation
            of brain acetylcholine synthesis.
          population: Biochemical, synaptosomal, and animal literature; no dietary human trial.
          result: >-
            Distinguished mitochondrial acetyl-CoA generation from cytosolic use by ChAT and identified
            several supported supply routes.
          effect_magnitude: No pooled dietary or clinical effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Establishes compartmented acetyl-CoA provision as a second upstream substrate-control problem.
          limitations: >-
            Older mechanistic literature; the relative contribution of proposed routes remains
            context-dependent.
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Szutowicz et al. (2010)
        citation_key: szutowicz_thiamine_acetylcoa_2010
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#szutowicz_thiamine_acetylcoa_2010
        data_level: Preclinical
        why_relevant: >-
          Pyrithiamine-induced thiamine deficiency reduced pyruvate-dehydrogenase flux and mitochondrial and
          cytosolic acetyl-CoA in rat nerve terminals, supporting the compartmented acetyl-unit supply model.
        why_excluded: >-
          The reported cholinergic endpoint was altered quantal acetylcholine release, while ChAT activity was
          unchanged; it does not establish vitamin B1 as a PM6 synthesis requirement or intake-responsive
          lever.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F3
    finding_label: Cholinergic biology is translationally relevant to attention
    finding_summary: >-
      Acetylcholine-receptor and choline-status findings sit near attention biology in ADHD-related samples.
      That is translational context, not an ADHD treatment rule.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Use these studies as attention-relevant cholinergic context. They do not show that choline
      supplementation treats ADHD.
    finding_statement: >-
      Human ADHD-related muscarinic-binding and choline-status evidence is translationally relevant to
      attention; it is not a demonstration that changing choline intake treats ADHD.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Lower muscarinic binding in boys with ADHD and choline-status discussion in a neurodevelopmental review
      together support a cholinergic context for attention. They do not isolate acetylcholine synthesis as a
      treatment target and they do not measure attention after a choline intervention designed to change
      synthesis.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      Cross-sectional receptor binding and a narrative review. No choline intervention arm for ADHD or
      attention scores is attached.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Johansson et al. (2013)
        citation_key: johansson_decreased_2013
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#johansson_decreased_2013
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          Decreased muscarinic binding in boys with ADHD supplies attention-relevant cholinergic context, not
          a treatment effect.
        assessment:
          study: Same fibroblast binding comparison used in PM6-F1, reused here for the attention relationship.
          population: Boys with ADHD and comparison boys.
          result: Lower muscarinic binding in the ADHD group.
          effect_magnitude: Binding contrast only; no attention-score change after diet.
          evidence_summary: Anchors the attention relationship in human cholinergic biology.
          limitations: Not brain imaging of acetylcholine and not a dietary trial.
      - label: Derbyshire and Maes (2023)
        citation_key: derbyshire_role_2023
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#derbyshire_role_2023
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          Altered choline status is discussed in ADHD-related literature without proving choline treatment of
          ADHD.
        assessment:
          study: Same narrative review used in PM6-F1 and PM6-F2, reused here for phenome context.
          population: ADHD and other neurodevelopmental subgroups summarised in the review.
          result: Discussed choline as a possible modifiable neurodevelopmental factor.
          effect_magnitude: No ADHD treatment-effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Supplies choline-status context for attention, not a dosing rule.
          limitations: Review synthesis; not a choline-for-ADHD trial.

    primary_phenome: Focus / Attention Stability

## 1. Mission & Overview + Dietary Levers

### Overview

Acetylcholine is made in nerve endings when choline is joined to acetyl-CoA, a cell-made acetate carrier. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) Diet can provide choline itself or choline from phosphatidylcholine, and vitamin B5 supports the acetyl-CoA side. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8) Entry into the nerve ending still controls access to the reaction. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) The reaction supplies acetylcholine for later cholinergic signalling. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[3]](#pm-ref-3)

- **Benefits:** Acetylcholine is the transmitter cholinergic circuits use for attention and learning. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[1]](#pm-ref-1) That biological role is not a shown gain in attention from more choline. [[1]](#pm-ref-1)
- **Implementation Notes:** Choline, phosphatidylcholine, and vitamin B5 are the provision routes. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8) Acetyl-CoA is made inside the cell and is not a dietary target. [[12]](#pm-ref-12) No dose is established for raising brain acetylcholine. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

↑ substrate availability in cholinergic terminals; ↑ capacity to synthesise acetylcholine

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Cholinergic signalling depends on a nerve terminal having both reaction substrates at the right place and time. Choline must first enter through a high-affinity transporter; choline acetyltransferase then transfers an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA. This synthesis capacity is different from the amount of acetylcholine stored, released, or detected at receptors.

<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (Choline entry is a regulated supply step)

Choline reaching the brain and choline entering a cholinergic nerve terminal are separate steps. CTL1/CTL2 transport systems operate at brain microvascular endothelium, whereas the high-affinity transporter CHT/SLC5A7 recovers choline into cholinergic nerve terminals. CHT activity and movement to the cell surface respond to neuronal activity, making terminal transport a major control point rather than a passive reflection of how much choline was eaten. Ojiakor and Rylett (2020) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) review terminal transport; Inazu (2019) [[13]](#pm-ref-13) reviews the blood–brain boundary.

#### (Two substrates form acetylcholine)

Inside the terminal, choline acetyltransferase transfers the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to choline, forming acetylcholine and coenzyme A. Choline and acetyl-CoA are therefore reaction substrates; the enzyme does not use folate, vitamin B12, or pantothenate directly as cofactors. Oda (1999) [[4]](#pm-ref-4) establishes the enzyme chemistry.

#### (Acetyl-CoA has its own compartmented supply route)

ChAT uses acetyl-CoA in the cytosol, but much neuronal acetyl-CoA is generated in mitochondria. Acetyl units can reach the cytosolic pool through routes including citrate export and ATP-citrate-lyase cleavage, alongside other proposed pyruvate-dependent or mitochondrial-export routes. Their relative contribution is not fully settled, but acetyl-CoA availability can regulate synthesis independently of choline transport. Jope (1979) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) reviews this evidence. It does not make glucose, pyruvate, citrate, or dietary acetyl-CoA separate requirements on this page.

#### (Dietary provision reaches the two substrates by different routes)

Phosphatidylcholine is a choline-containing dietary form. Human tracer evidence shows that it is digested and remodelled, with labelled choline appearing in plasma; it is therefore a provision route to choline, not another ChAT substrate. Böckmann et al. (2023) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) measured this route. Pantothenate supports the other side of the reaction by supplying coenzyme A for acetyl-CoA formation. Severe pantothenate depletion reduced labelled brain acetylcholine synthesis in a chronic rat model, and pantothenate co-administration increased it. Rivera-Calimlim et al. (1988) [[8]](#pm-ref-8) do not establish a routine human supplementation effect.

#### (A shared one-carbon resource can change choline availability)

Choline can also be oxidised to betaine for one-carbon metabolism (the network that transfers methyl groups). Folate compromise and genetic impairment of B12-dependent methionine-cycle function lowered brain choline and acetylcholine in animal models, although regional responses were not uniform. Chan et al. (2008) [[9]](#pm-ref-9), Crivello et al. (2010) [[10]](#pm-ref-10), and Jadavji et al. (2014) [[11]](#pm-ref-11) support a shared-resource constraint, not a claim that folate, B12, or betaine run the ChAT reaction.

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

Synthesis ends when acetylcholine has been formed. Packaging by the vesicular acetylcholine transporter, release into the synapse, receptor binding, breakdown by acetylcholinesterase, and the resulting cognitive effects are later stages. Acetylcholine concentration also reflects storage, release, and breakdown, so concentration alone is not a synthesis-rate measurement.

#### (Integration within BRS1)

This synthesis capacity supports [BRS1(FM2) — Cholinergic Function](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm2/brs1-fm2-cholinergic-function). Choline allocation also intersects BRS2 remethylation and phosphatidylcholine biology, while the [BRS2(KC1) — Methyl Donor Pool](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/kc/brs2-kc1-one-carbon-donor-pool) can constrain how much choline remains available for the synthesis substrate pool.

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Transporter evidence identifies terminal choline uptake as a control step for acetylcholine synthesis, while human tracing demonstrates systemic assimilation of choline from dietary phosphatidylcholine. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Animal depletion and rescue studies support bounded pantothenate and one-carbon dependencies, with acetylcholine responses varying by experimental condition, region and age. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) [[9]](#pm-ref-9) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) The evidence therefore supports provision and local synthesis capacity without equating plasma choline delivery with neuronal release, attention benefit or a human dose response.

scientific_findings_intro: >-
  Human structure and mutagenesis studies establish BHMT’s betaine-dependent reaction and catalytic zinc
  requirement. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Controlled human choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and
  worsened the homocysteine response to a methionine challenge in participants who developed hepatic
  steatosis; repletion restored that response. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Animal depletion and enzyme-inhibition studies
  complement this supported dependency chain, but human tissue BHMT flux and cognitive outcomes were not
  measured. [[12]](#pm-ref-12) [[13]](#pm-ref-13)
scientific_findings:
  - id: PM2-F1
    finding_label: BHMT remethylates homocysteine with betaine and catalytic zinc
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Human betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase (BHMT) transfers one methyl group from betaine to
      homocysteine. The products are methionine and dimethylglycine. A zinc ion bound by three cysteines
      activates homocysteine. Folate and vitamin B12 are not part of this reaction.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      This is the reaction boundary. It does not include folate-dependent remethylation, the later conversion
      of methionine to SAMe, whole-cycle throughput, phosphatidylethanolamine methyltransferase, or
      acetylcholine formation. It also does not show that dietary zinc intake changes the reaction in people.
    finding_statement: >-
      BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine, forming methionine and dimethylglycine,
      without folate or vitamin B12 in that reaction, and uses an active-site zinc ion to activate
      homocysteine.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Human crystal structures show that BHMT makes methionine from betaine and homocysteine and uses zinc to
      activate homocysteine. Mutating any of the three zinc-binding cysteines to alanine abolishes activity
      and sharply reduces zinc binding, and the same biochemical work states the products as methionine and
      dimethylglycine. A methyl-donor review states that methyl flow through this pathway does not depend on
      folate or vitamin B12. Together these sources identify the reaction and its metal. They do not test
      ordinary dietary control or human tissue flux.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The enzyme evidence uses purified or recombinant human protein, not intact human metabolism. Loss of
      activity after removing zinc ligands does not show that dietary zinc usually limits the enzyme. The
      review statement that the pathway is independent of folate and vitamin B12 is not a new flux experiment.
      Quantitative claims in that review about choline deficiency and liver methionine were not re-checked in
      the primary animal papers.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Evans et al. (2002)
        citation_key: evans_betaine_2002
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#evans_betaine_2002
        data_level: Cellular / Molecular
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Human BHMT structures show methionine formation from betaine and homocysteine, with zinc activating
          homocysteine; oxidation that expels zinc rearranges the active site.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            X-ray structures of human BHMT in an oxidised zinc-free form and a reduced zinc-bound form with a
            homocysteine-like bisubstrate analog.
          population: Purified crystallised human BHMT; no cells, animals or human participants.
          result: >-
            The enzyme forms methionine from betaine and homocysteine. Zinc activates homocysteine. The
            zinc-binding sequences sit at the ends of barrel strands, and a Cys217–Cys299 disulfide expels
            zinc.
          effect_magnitude: Structures at 2.15 Å (zinc-free) and 2.05 Å (zinc-bound). No physiological effect size applies.
          evidence_summary: Direct structural evidence for the human reaction and for catalytic zinc.
          limitations: >-
            Static structures establish catalytic geometry, not in-vivo flux, dietary zinc responsiveness, or
            a clinical outcome.
      - label: Breksa and Garrow (1999)
        citation_key: breksa_zinc_1999
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#breksa_zinc_1999
        data_level: Cellular / Molecular
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Replacing any of Cys217, Cys299 or Cys300 with alanine abolished human BHMT activity and reduced
          zinc binding. The reaction produces methionine and dimethylglycine from betaine and homocysteine.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Site-directed mutagenesis of recombinant human liver BHMT, with activity and zinc-binding
            measurements.
          population: Recombinant human BHMT protein expressed in bacteria; no human participants.
          result: >-
            Cys217, Cys299 and Cys300 were identified as zinc ligands. Mutation of any one to alanine caused
            complete loss of activity and a significant reduction in zinc binding. The catalysed transfer is
            from betaine to homocysteine, yielding dimethylglycine and methionine.
          effect_magnitude: Complete loss of activity for each alanine substitution. No human effect size applies.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Direct evidence that catalytic activity of human BHMT depends on those zinc ligands, and a clear
            statement of the reaction products.
          limitations: >-
            Bacterial expression and purified-protein assays do not show that dietary zinc limits BHMT in
            human tissues.
      - label: Obeid (2013)
        citation_key: obeid_metabolic_2013
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#obeid_metabolic_2013
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Methyl-group flow through BHMT does not depend on folate or vitamin B12, although the pathway is
          most active in liver and kidney and talks to the folate route.
        assessment:
          study: Narrative review of methyl-donor deficiency with emphasis on the BHMT pathway.
          population: Review of human and animal methyl-donor studies; not a new experiment.
          result: >-
            BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine. The review states that methyl flow
            through this pathway is not dependent on folate or vitamin B12, while several cross-talk
            mechanisms exist. BHMT is particularly active in liver and kidney.
          effect_magnitude: No new effect size. The review cites other studies for homocysteine and metabolite changes.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Explicit pathway-level statement that folate and vitamin B12 are not required for methyl flow
            through BHMT.
          limitations: >-
            A review cannot replace a flux assay. Some quantitative deficiency claims are attributed to other
            papers and were not re-adjudicated here.
    evidence_dependency:
      - >-
        Obeid (2013) is also primary evidence in PM2-F2 for choline oxidation. That reuse is one review, not a
        second experiment.
  - id: PM2-F2
    finding_label: Choline oxidation supplies betaine and is not the BHMT reaction
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Choline can be oxidised to betaine aldehyde and then to betaine. That sequence can supply the BHMT
      substrate. It is not the methyl transfer that BHMT carries out, and betaine is not turned back into
      choline.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Choline is a precursor of the substrate, not a cofactor or substrate of BHMT. Acetylcholine formation
      and phosphatidylethanolamine methylation use choline or SAMe in other reactions.
    finding_statement: >-
      Irreversible oxidation of choline to betaine is an upstream supply route for the BHMT substrate and is
      not itself the BHMT reaction.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      A methyl-donor review states that betaine is produced by irreversible oxidation of choline through
      choline dehydrogenase and betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, and that BHMT then uses betaine. A
      choline-dehydrogenase review places the human enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane, mainly in
      kidney and liver, and separates the first oxidation to betaine aldehyde from the second oxidation to
      betaine. Betaine then donates a methyl group in the homocysteine-to-methionine reaction. The two steps
      are supply, not the BHMT reaction.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      Purified, stable human choline dehydrogenase has been difficult to obtain, so some catalytic detail is
      inferred from related enzymes and from tissue activity rather than from a complete human kinetic
      characterisation. The reviews do not show that raising choline intake increases BHMT flux in people.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Obeid (2013)
        citation_key: obeid_metabolic_2013
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#obeid_metabolic_2013
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Betaine can be formed by irreversible oxidation of choline via choline dehydrogenase and
          betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, and BHMT then uses that betaine to remethylate homocysteine.
        assessment:
          study: Narrative review of methyl-donor metabolism centred on BHMT.
          population: Review of human and animal evidence; not a new enzyme assay.
          result: >-
            The review states the two-enzyme oxidation of choline to betaine and the subsequent BHMT reaction.
            It treats the oxidation as irreversible.
          effect_magnitude: No new effect size for the oxidation steps.
          evidence_summary: Pathway-level evidence that choline oxidation supplies betaine upstream of BHMT.
          limitations: >-
            Review synthesis, not a direct demonstration of human choline dehydrogenase kinetics or of dietary
            choline increasing BHMT flux.
      - label: Salvi and Gadda (2013)
        citation_key: salvi_choline_2013
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#salvi_choline_2013
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Human choline dehydrogenase oxidises choline to betaine aldehyde, and betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase
          completes formation of betaine, which can donate a methyl group to homocysteine.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Review of human choline dehydrogenase localisation, physiological role and biochemical
            characterisation.
          population: Review of human tissue activity and comparative biochemistry; not a dietary trial.
          result: >-
            The enzyme sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and is found mainly in kidney and liver. It
            oxidises choline to betaine aldehyde. A second enzyme, betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, oxidises
            that aldehyde to betaine. Betaine is described as a methyl donor for methionine formation from
            homocysteine. Purified active human enzyme has been difficult to obtain.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            Tissue activity was reported mainly in kidney, with about six-fold lower activity in liver. No
            dietary dose-response was measured.
          evidence_summary: Enzyme-level support for the two-step oxidation that supplies betaine.
          limitations: >-
            Incomplete purification of human choline dehydrogenase limits kinetic detail. Localisation and
            pathway role do not show that dietary choline changes BHMT flux.
    evidence_dependency:
      - >-
        Obeid (2013) is also primary evidence in PM2-F1 for folate- and vitamin B12-independence of BHMT. That
        reuse is one review, not a second experiment.
  - id: PM2-IC1
    finding_label: Plasma homocysteine is not tissue BHMT flux
    presentation: interpretive-constraint
    finding_summary: >-
      Betaine supplements lower plasma homocysteine, and severe choline depletion can raise it after a
      methionine load. The same blood measurement also falls after vitamin B12 and fish oil, which are not
      BHMT substrates. The number is not the enzyme's rate in tissue and is not a clinical benefit.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      A homocysteine change can be consistent with this route and still fail to prove it. Read supplement and
      depletion studies as blood results unless enzyme activity or traced methyl flux was measured.
    finding_statement: >-
      Changes in plasma homocysteine after betaine supplementation, choline depletion, or vitamin B12 and
      fish-oil treatment do not measure tissue BHMT flux and do not establish a clinical benefit of this
      reaction.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      In healthy adults, six weeks of supplemental betaine lowered fasting plasma homocysteine relative to
      placebo, and it also blunted the rise after a methionine load. The authors inferred faster
      betaine-dependent remethylation, but they did not measure BHMT activity, tissue methionine formation or
      dimethylglycine flux. In mice, choline deficiency doubled post-load plasma homocysteine, and a small
      male pilot found a higher post-load value after clinical choline depletion, yet mouse liver betaine did
      not fall and BHMT was not assayed. A separate trial lowered plasma homocysteine with vitamin B12, fish
      oil or both, without betaine. The biomarker is therefore real, shared and non-specific.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The betaine trial selected healthy adults with relatively high homocysteine still in a broad reference
      range. The human choline study was a pilot of eight men. None of the three studies measured tissue BHMT
      flux, attention or cognition.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Olthof et al. (2003)
        citation_key: olthof_low_2003
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#olthof_low_2003
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          Daily betaine at 1.5, 3 and 6 g lowered fasting plasma homocysteine by about 12%, 15% and 20% versus
          placebo after six weeks, without a measurement of tissue BHMT flux.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Randomised, placebo-controlled trial of anhydrous betaine for six weeks, with methionine-load
            tests.
          population: >-
            Four groups of 19 healthy adults selected for higher plasma homocysteine within a broad reference
            range.
          result: >-
            Fasting plasma homocysteine after 1.5, 3 and 6 g/day was about 12%, 15% and 20% lower than
            placebo. The post-load rise was also smaller. The discussion infers increased betaine-dependent
            remethylation.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            About 12% (P < 0.01), 15% (P < 0.002) and 20% (P < 0.0001) lower fasting homocysteine than placebo
            at six weeks for 1.5, 3 and 6 g/day.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Direct human evidence that supplemental betaine lowers plasma homocysteine. The endpoint is a
            circulating metabolite, not enzyme flux.
          limitations: >-
            No BHMT activity, tissue methionine flux, dimethylglycine production rate, or clinical symptom
            outcome was measured.
      - label: da Costa et al. (2005)
        citation_key: da_costa_choline_2005
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#da_costa_choline_2005
        data_level: Mixed
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Choline deficiency raised post-methionine-load plasma homocysteine in mice and in a small human
          pilot, but did not measure BHMT activity, and mouse liver betaine did not fall.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Three-week mouse diets with 0, 10 or 35 mmol choline/kg, plus a depletion-repletion pilot in men,
            each with an oral methionine load.
          population: Male C57BL/6J mice and eight healthy men aged 20–46 years.
          result: >-
            Two hours after the load, choline-deficient mice had about twice the plasma homocysteine of
            choline-fed mice. Fasting values did not differ. Four hours after the load, clinically
            choline-depleted men had plasma homocysteine about 35% higher than when not depleted. Hepatic
            betaine in the mice was not significantly lower.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            About twofold higher post-load homocysteine in deficient mice. About 35% higher post-load
            homocysteine in depleted men. Mouse liver betaine 1.3 ± 0.3 versus 1.1 ± 0.3 nmol/mg protein.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Dietary choline depletion can change post-load plasma homocysteine. It does not isolate BHMT flux,
            and the mouse betaine pool was not shown to fall.
          limitations: >-
            Human sample of eight men, clinical depletion rather than ordinary intake, and no enzyme or tracer
            measurement.
      - label: Huang et al. (2015)
        citation_key: tao_huang_effect_2015
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#tao_huang_effect_2015
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          Vitamin B12, fish oil and their combination lowered plasma homocysteine without any betaine
          intervention, so the biomarker is not specific to BHMT.
        assessment:
          study: Randomised trial of vitamin B12, fish oil, or both, with plasma homocysteine as an endpoint.
          population: Thirty-eight participants randomised to three groups.
          result: >-
            The repository abstract reports plasma homocysteine reductions of about 22% with vitamin B12, 19%
            with fish oil, and 39% with the combination. Betaine and BHMT were not the interventions.
          effect_magnitude: About 22%, 19% and 39% lower plasma homocysteine in the three arms.
          evidence_summary: Shows that plasma homocysteine can fall through inputs that are not the BHMT substrate.
          limitations: >-
            The attached abstract does not report BHMT activity, betaine status or a clinical neurological
            outcome. Design detail beyond the abstract was not re-extracted.
  - id: PM2-F3
    finding_label: ADHD diet reviews do not test BHMT
    presentation: phenome-relationship
    primary_phenome: Focus / Attention Stability
    finding_summary: >-
      The attached attention reviews discuss dietary patterns, supplements and choline in neurodevelopment.
      They do not measure BHMT or test betaine as a treatment for attention.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      An attention relationship can remain a framework bridge. It should not be read as evidence that this
      remethylation route changes focus.
    finding_statement: >-
      The repository ADHD diet review and choline neurodevelopment review do not directly demonstrate that
      BHMT-dependent remethylation changes Focus / Attention Stability.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-

  - id: PM2-F5
    finding_label: Betaine availability and choline supply can constrain remethylation reserve
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Controlled human choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and reduced challenged remethylation reserve
      in participants who developed clinical depletion. In rats, choline deprivation lowered hepatic betaine
      and the phenotype was suppressed by choline or betaine; specific BHMT inhibition independently produced
      the expected pathway failure.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Together with the established BHMT reaction, these intervention, pool, rescue and specific-inhibition
      edges support a constraint on betaine-dependent remethylation capacity. They do not directly measure
      human tissue BHMT flux or show a benefit from intake above adequacy.
    finding_statement: >-
      Inadequate betaine availability, including from conditional failure of choline provision, can constrain
      BHMT-dependent homocysteine remethylation capacity.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Da Costa et al. fed eight healthy men a 550 mg/day choline baseline diet followed by 50 mg/day for up to
      42 days. Plasma choline and betaine fell by about 30% and 47% while folate remained adequate. In the
      four participants who developed hepatic steatosis, post-load homocysteine was 5.2 µmol/L higher and
      returned to the baseline response after repletion. In rats under low-methionine conditions, Setoue et
      al. found that choline deprivation markedly lowered hepatic betaine and raised plasma homocysteine,
      while either choline or betaine restored hepatic betaine and suppressed the increase. Strakova et al.
      independently showed that a specific BHMT inhibitor reduced liver BHMT activity by more than 90%, raised
      plasma homocysteine two- to five-fold and lowered liver SAM by more than 40%. Human BHMT biochemistry
      establishes betaine as the methyl donor. These edges form a supported constraint chain.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The human study was a pilot in eight men, with the challenged response confined to four clinically
      depleted participants. The pool-rescue and specific-inhibition evidence is from rat liver, and neither
      study measured isotope-resolved human BHMT flux. Choline partitioning, endogenous synthesis and
      methionine/folate state modify the provision route. The chain supports capacity constraint under
      demonstrated depletion, not universal limitation on ordinary diets, benefit from supplementation above
      adequacy, or a cognitive outcome.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: da Costa et al. (2005)
        citation_key: da_costa_choline_2005
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#da_costa_choline_2005
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Controlled choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and reduced post-methionine-load
          homocysteine-handling reserve in the participants who developed clinical depletion; both the
          phenotype and challenge response reversed with repletion.
        assessment:
          study: Controlled depletion–repletion pilot with a methionine-load challenge.
          population: Eight healthy men aged 20–46 years; four developed hepatic steatosis during depletion.
          result: >-
            Plasma choline and betaine fell about 30% and 47% in the full group. In the four clinically
            depleted men, post-load homocysteine increased by 5.2 µmol/L (95% CI 1.2–9.1; P = 0.025) relative
            to the 550 mg/day baseline phase and returned to the baseline response after repletion. Folate did
            not fall.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            Betaine fell from 66 ± 7 to 35 ± 2 nmol/mL in all eight men; clinically depleted participants had
            a 5.2 µmol/L greater post-load homocysteine response.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Human intervention evidence linking choline inadequacy, lower betaine availability and reduced
            remethylation reserve under challenge.
          limitations: >-
            Small male-only pilot, severe controlled depletion, shared circulating endpoint, and no direct
            tissue or isotope-resolved BHMT flux.
      - label: Evans et al. (2002)
        citation_key: evans_betaine_2002
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#evans_betaine_2002
        data_level: Cellular / Molecular
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Human BHMT structures establish the betaine-to-homocysteine methyl transfer that links betaine
          availability to the challenged remethylation response.
        assessment:
          study: X-ray structural analysis of human BHMT.
          population: Purified human BHMT; no participants.
          result: BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine to form methionine and dimethylglycine.
          effect_magnitude: No human intervention effect size.
          evidence_summary: Provides reaction-specific attribution for the donor-pool intervention chain.
          limitations: Purified-enzyme evidence does not itself establish dietary constraint.
      - label: Setoue et al. (2008)
        citation_key: setoue_choline_deprivation_2008
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#setoue_choline_deprivation_2008
        data_level: Preclinical
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Under low-methionine conditions, choline deprivation depleted hepatic betaine and raised plasma
          homocysteine; either choline or betaine suppressed the phenotype.
        assessment:
          study: Controlled rat feeding experiments varying choline, methionine context and lipotrope rescue.
          population: Male Wistar rats fed casein- or soybean-protein-based diets.
          result: >-
            On the choline-deprived soybean-protein diet, hepatic betaine fell from about 3.65 to 0.13 µmol/g
            and plasma homocysteine rose from about 12.5 to 33.5 µmol/L. Choline or betaine supplementation
            restored hepatic betaine to about 9.81 or 13.3 µmol/g and lowered plasma homocysteine to about 7.3
            or 7.7 µmol/L. Ex-vivo BHMT activity did not decline.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            Approximately 96% lower hepatic betaine with deprivation; rescue restored the pool above control
            and suppressed hyperhomocysteinaemia.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Pool depletion and rescue connect conditional choline inadequacy to loss of substrate-supported
            remethylation capacity rather than loss of BHMT protein competence.
          limitations: >-
            Rat liver model under low-methionine conditions; homocysteine removal also involved
            transsulfuration, and no in-vivo isotope-resolved BHMT flux was measured.
      - label: Strakova et al. (2011)
        citation_key: strakova_bhmt_inhibition_2011
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#strakova_bhmt_inhibition_2011
        data_level: Preclinical
        exposure_context: isolated-substance
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Specific pharmacological BHMT inhibition produced the pathway direction expected when BHMT-dependent
          capacity fails.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Rat feeding study using the potent and specific BHMT inhibitor S-(δ-carboxybutyl)-L-homocysteine
            for 3 or 14 days across adequate, cysteine-free and methionine-deficient diets.
          population: Rats; no human participants.
          result: >-
            The inhibitor reduced liver BHMT activity by more than 90%, increased plasma homocysteine two- to
            five-fold and lowered hepatic SAM by more than 40% across dietary conditions.
          effect_magnitude: '>90% lower BHMT activity; 2–5-fold higher plasma homocysteine; >40% lower liver SAM.'
          evidence_summary: >-
            Specific perturbation confirms that impaired BHMT capacity can generate the observed remethylation
            and methylation-state direction.
          limitations: >-
            Pharmacological inhibition in rats does not quantify the effect of ordinary human betaine or
            choline intake.
    evidence_dependency:
      - >-
        Da Costa et al. (2005) is also used in PM2-IC1. PM2-IC1 establishes that plasma homocysteine alone is
        non-specific; PM2-F5 relies on the combined depletion, pool, challenge, repletion and reaction chain
        rather than treating that biomarker alone as BHMT flux.
      - >-
        Evans et al. (2002) is also primary evidence in PM2-F1. Its reuse in PM2-F5 supplies the same
        reaction-specific link and is not independent replication.

### Overview

Betaine–homocysteine methyltransferase transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine, forming methionine and dimethylglycine. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) A bound zinc ion activates homocysteine. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Folate and vitamin B12 are not part of that reaction. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) Betaine may come from the diet or from oxidation of choline. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[4]](#pm-ref-4) In healthy men, controlled choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and reduced homocysteine-handling reserve, and repletion reversed that change. [[6]](#pm-ref-6)

- **Benefits:** This route replenishes methionine, and with it the capacity to handle a homocysteine load, without using folate or vitamin B12. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) In the men who became clinically depleted, that reserve fell with the betaine pool and returned after repletion. [[6]](#pm-ref-6)
- **Implementation Notes:** Betaine and choline are the provision routes. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) The bound zinc ion is part of the enzyme, not a dietary zinc target. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Choline depletion lowered the betaine pool; that study does not set a dose for people whose supply is already adequate. [[6]](#pm-ref-6)
- **Biological Relevance:** [Folate- and vitamin B12-dependent remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation) is a neighbouring reaction, not this methyl transfer. [[3]](#pm-ref-3)

## 4. Mechanistic Basis + Scientific Findings

### Summary

Homocysteine (an amino acid left after methyl groups are used) can be turned back into methionine by a betaine-dependent reaction that does not use folate or vitamin B12. The methionine can later be used to make SAMe, but this reaction stops at methionine. A fall in plasma homocysteine after betaine is taken is a blood result, not a measurement of how fast the enzyme is working in tissue.

<span id="pm2-mechanism-f1" />
<span id="the-methyl-transfer" />

#### PM2-F1

BHMT moves one methyl group from betaine (trimethylglycine) onto homocysteine. The products are methionine and dimethylglycine (what remains of betaine after that methyl group leaves) [Breksa and Garrow (1999) [[2]](#pm-ref-2); Evans et al. (2002) [[1]](#pm-ref-1)]. A zinc ion held by three cysteines in the active site activates the homocysteine thiol. Changing any of those cysteines to alanine abolishes activity in the recombinant human enzyme [[2]](#pm-ref-2). Human structures capture both a zinc-free oxidised form and a zinc-bound form [[1]](#pm-ref-1).


Supporting evidence: [PM2-F1](#pm2-f1).

#### (What the reaction does not use)

Folate and vitamin B12 are required by the parallel methionine-synthase route. They are not substrates or cofactors of this transfer. Methyl flow through BHMT does not depend on them [Obeid (2013) [[3]](#pm-ref-3)]. The enzyme is especially active in liver and kidney rather than throughout the brain [[2]](#pm-ref-2), [[3]](#pm-ref-3).

<span id="pm2-mechanism-f2" />
<span id="choline-is-a-supply-route" />

#### PM2-F2

Choline can be oxidised to betaine aldehyde by choline dehydrogenase, then to betaine by betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase. That oxidation is irreversible, so it can feed betaine into BHMT without being the BHMT reaction itself [Obeid (2013) [[3]](#pm-ref-3); Salvi and Gadda (2013) [[4]](#pm-ref-4)]. Human choline dehydrogenase sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and is found mainly in kidney and liver [[4]](#pm-ref-4).


Supporting evidence: [PM2-F2](#pm2-f2).

<span id="pm2-mechanism-f5" />

#### PM2-F5

Inadequate betaine availability, including from conditional failure of choline provision, can constrain BHMT-dependent homocysteine remethylation capacity. Evans et al. (2002) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); da Costa et al. (2005) [[6]](#pm-ref-6); Setoue et al. (2008) [[12]](#pm-ref-12); Strakova et al. (2011) [[13]](#pm-ref-13)

Supporting evidence: [PM2-F5](#pm2-f5).

#### (Plasma homocysteine is a shared marker)

In healthy adults, 1.5–6 g/day of supplemental betaine lowered fasting plasma homocysteine over six weeks [Olthof et al. (2003) [[5]](#pm-ref-5)]. Experimental choline depletion raised homocysteine after a methionine load in mice and in a pilot of eight men, without a fall in mouse liver betaine and without an enzyme assay [da Costa et al. (2005) [[6]](#pm-ref-6)]. Vitamin B12 and fish oil also lower plasma homocysteine, so the same blood result is not specific to this enzyme [Huang et al. (2015) [[7]](#pm-ref-7)].

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

This PM is the betaine-dependent methyl transfer only.

Folate/B12-dependent remethylation belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM1](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation). Methionine-to-SAMe conversion belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM3](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis). Combined cycle throughput belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM4](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm4-methionine-cycle-flux).

SAMe-dependent phosphatidylethanolamine methylation belongs to [BRS2-FM3-PM7](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm3/brs2-fm3-pm7-phosphatidylcholine-formation). Acetylcholine formation from choline belongs to [BRS1-FM2-PM6](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm2/brs1-fm2-pm6-acetylcholine-synthesis-support).

#### (Integration within BRS2)

Within [BRS2(FM1) — Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency), this reaction is one way to regenerate methionine when the folate-dependent route is under strain [Obeid (2013) [[3]](#pm-ref-3)]. The methionine can enter SAMe formation afterwards. Whether a shortfall in the wider methyl-donor pool limits the enzyme's activity in people has not been shown, because plasma homocysteine does not measure that activity [[5]](#pm-ref-5), [[6]](#pm-ref-6).

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Human structure and mutagenesis studies establish BHMT’s betaine-dependent reaction and catalytic zinc requirement. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Controlled human choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and worsened the homocysteine response to a methionine challenge in participants who developed hepatic steatosis; repletion restored that response. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Animal depletion and enzyme-inhibition studies complement this supported dependency chain, but human tissue BHMT flux and cognitive outcomes were not measured. ## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections

### 5.1 BRS Pathways

**BRS2-FM1-PM2 — Betaine/BHMT Remethylation**<br />
↓<br />
[BRS2-FM1-PM3 — SAMe Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis)

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS1-FM2-PM6 — Acetylcholine Synthesis Support](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm2/brs1-fm2-pm6-acetylcholine-synthesis-support) — Choline that is oxidised becomes betaine for this methyl transfer, while choline that is not oxidised is the substrate used to make acetylcholine. Betaine is not converted back to choline, so this shared use of choline does not show that dietary betaine raises brain acetylcholine.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS2-FM1-PM1 — Folate/B12-Dependent Homocysteine Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation) — This sibling regenerates methionine from homocysteine by methionine synthase, using a folate-derived methyl group and vitamin B12. BHMT uses betaine instead, so the routes are parallel and folate is not a cofactor of this reaction.
- [BRS2-FM1-PM3 — SAMe Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis) — Methionine produced here can be joined to ATP by methionine adenosyltransferase to form the later methyl donor. That conversion is a separate enzyme step and is not catalysed by BHMT.
- [BRS2-FM1-PM4 — Methionine Cycle Flux](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm4-methionine-cycle-flux) — The wider methionine cycle combines remethylation, methyl-group use and regeneration into one throughput. This PM is only the betaine-dependent remethylation step, not that combined throughput.

  Human tracer studies show context-dependent substrate responsiveness. Removing methionine and cysteine
  together reduced whole-blood glutathione synthesis, whereas removing cysteine with methionine kept adequate
  did not reduce erythrocyte synthesis in young men. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) In older adults with
  lower baseline synthesis, combined N-acetylcysteine and glycine supplementation raised erythrocyte

  dietary cysteine limitation; blood-cell measurements do not establish neuronal synthesis or clinical
  benefit.
scientific_findings:
  - id: PM6-F1
    finding_label: Two ATP-dependent enzymes assemble glutathione
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Glutamate-cysteine ligase joins glutamate and cysteine using ATP. Glutathione synthetase then adds
      glycine, again using ATP, and binds magnesium. Selenium-dependent peroxidase activity and
      riboflavin-derived FAD in glutathione reductase are not part of these assembly reactions.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Glutamate, cysteine, glycine and ATP are the assembly substrates. Magnesium participates in the second
      enzyme. ATP and magnesium are intracellular biochemical requirements, not dietary levers. Selenium and
      riboflavin support later use and recycling of glutathione.
    finding_statement: >-
      Glutathione synthesis requires ATP-dependent formation of γ-glutamylcysteine from glutamate and
      cysteine, followed by ATP-dependent addition of glycine, and does not use selenium or riboflavin as
      synthesis substrates.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Reviewed catalytic annotation of purified human glutamate-cysteine ligase records ATP-dependent ligation
      of L-glutamate and L-cysteine as the first step. Human glutathione synthetase structural work records
      ATP-dependent addition of glycine and one bound magnesium ion per subunit as the second step. Together
      they define the assembly boundary. Human glutathione peroxidase uses an active-site selenocysteine to
      reduce peroxides with glutathione already formed, and glutathione reductase binds FAD while reducing
      glutathione disulfide. Those enzymes consume or restore glutathione; they do not assemble it.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The enzyme evidence is purified protein and structure, not intact human flux. A lower cysteine Km on the
      first enzyme does not prove that ordinary diets are cysteine-limited. Magnesium binding does not show
      that magnesium intake changes synthesis. The dietary review that groups selenium and riboflavin with
      glutathione support does not move those cofactors into the assembly reactions.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Misra and Griffith (1998)
        citation_key: misra_human_gcl_1998
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#misra_human_gcl_1998
        data_level: Cellular / Molecular
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Purified human glutamate-cysteine ligase catalyses ATP-dependent ligation of L-glutamate and
          L-cysteine, the first step of glutathione biosynthesis.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Expression and purification of human gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase, with catalytic constants
            recorded in the reviewed human GCLC entry that cites this paper.
          population: Purified human enzyme; no human participants.
          result: >-
            The reaction consumes L-glutamate, L-cysteine and ATP to form γ-glutamylcysteine, ADP and
            phosphate. The cited annotation reports Km values of 0.1 mM for L-cysteine, 1.8 mM for L-glutamate
            and 0.4 mM for ATP.
          effect_magnitude: Purified-enzyme Km values only; no human synthesis-rate effect.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Direct human-enzyme evidence for the first ATP-dependent assembly step and its amino-acid and ATP
            substrates.
          limitations: >-
            In-vitro constants do not establish in-vivo limitation, dietary responsiveness, tissue differences
            or clinical effects.
      - label: Polekhina et al. (1999)
        citation_key: polekhina_gss_1999
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#polekhina_gss_1999
        data_level: Cellular / Molecular
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Human glutathione synthetase produces glutathione from γ-glutamylcysteine and glycine in an
          ATP-dependent reaction and binds one magnesium ion per subunit.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Crystal structure of human glutathione synthetase at 2.10 Å in complex with ADP and glutathione,
            with catalytic and cofactor annotation.
          population: Crystallised human glutathione synthetase; no human participants.
          result: >-
            The structure and catalytic annotation place glycine and ATP in the second assembly step and
            record one Mg2+ ion bound per subunit.
          effect_magnitude: 2.10 Å structure; no physiological effect size.
          evidence_summary: Direct structural evidence for the second ATP-dependent step and its magnesium ion.
          limitations: >-
            A product-bound structure establishes catalytic participants, not dietary dose response or in-vivo
            flux.
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Minich et al. (2019)
        citation_key: minich_glutathione_2019
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#minich_glutathione_2019
        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: >-
          Reviews dietary nutrients discussed for glutathione support, including sulfur amino acids, selenium
          and riboflavin.
        why_excluded: >-
          It is a narrative review and does not itself measure the ligase reactions, ATP use, or separation of

      - label: Mullenbach et al. (1987)
        citation_key: mullenbach_gpx_selenocysteine_1987

        data_level: Cellular / Molecular

          Shows that human glutathione peroxidase encodes an active-site selenocysteine, so selenium belongs

        why_relevant: >-
