  - id: PM6-F2
    finding_label: Blood-cell synthesis responds only under defined substrate conditions
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Removing both methionine and cysteine slowed whole-blood glutathione synthesis in healthy young men.
      Combined cysteine-precursor and glycine supplementation raised erythrocyte synthesis in older adults. A
      methionine-adequate diet without cysteine did not lower erythrocyte synthesis in young men.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Substrate supply can change blood-cell synthesis in these specific conditions. That does not mean every
      ordinary diet is cysteine-limited, and the older-adult result is a supplemental precursor plus glycine,
      not a food prescription.
    finding_statement: >-
      Human blood-cell glutathione synthesis can slow when dietary methionine and cysteine are both removed
      and can rise in older adults after combined cysteine and glycine precursor supplementation, whereas a
      methionine-adequate cysteine-free diet did not limit erythrocyte synthesis in young men.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Three human tracer studies set the ceiling. In seven healthy young men, a 10-day amino-acid diet with
      methionine and cysteine removed lowered whole-blood fractional synthesis from 0.65 ± 0.13 to 0.49 ± 0.13
      per day and lowered absolute synthesis by about 23%, while concentration stayed near 1.2 mM and glycine
      intake was not reduced. In eight older adults compared with eight younger adults, erythrocyte
      glutathione synthesis and concentration were lower, and two weeks of cysteine plus glycine precursor
      supplementation raised fractional synthesis by 78.8% and absolute synthesis by 230.9%. The cysteine
      source in that protocol is N-acetylcysteine, given with glycine. In four young men, cysteine intakes
      from zero to 40 mg/kg/day did not change erythrocyte synthesis when methionine was held at 14 mg/kg/day.
      Synthesis is therefore substrate-responsive under defined restrictions, not universally limited by
      dietary cysteine.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      All three studies measured blood-cell, not neuronal, synthesis. The sulfur-amino-acid-free diet was an
      experimental amino-acid formula in seven young men for 10 days. The older-adult increase required
      combined supplementation and was not an isolated N-acetylcysteine or glycine test, not an ADHD trial,
      and not ordinary food. The cysteine-free arm used only four young men and two days of adaptation.
      Concentration did not track synthesis rate in the sulfur-amino-acid-free study.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Lyons et al. (2000)
        citation_key: lyons_glutathione_2000
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#lyons_glutathione_2000
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          A sulfur-amino-acid-free amino-acid diet slowed whole-blood glutathione synthesis in healthy young
          men without lowering glutathione concentration.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Randomised crossover of two 10-day L-amino-acid diets, adequate versus methionine and cysteine
            both set to zero, with a primed intravenous L-[1-13C]cysteine infusion on day 10.
          population: Seven healthy men, age 24 ± 6 years.
          result: >-
            Fractional synthesis fell from 0.65 ± 0.13 to 0.49 ± 0.13 per day (P < 0.01). Absolute synthesis
            fell from 747 ± 216 to 578.6 ± 135 µmol/L/day (P < 0.05), about 23%. Whole-blood glutathione
            stayed about 1.2 mM (1,142 ± 243 versus 1,216 ± 162 µM). Glycine in the formula rose from 39.6 to
            75.1 mg/kg/day so nitrogen stayed constant; glutamic acid was unchanged.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            About a 23% lower absolute synthesis rate after 10 days without methionine and cysteine;
            concentration unchanged.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Direct human evidence that removing the shared sulfur-amino-acid supply slows whole-blood
            glutathione synthesis.
          limitations: >-
            Experimental formula, young men, short duration, whole blood rather than brain, and no clinical
            outcome. Glycine was increased, so the slowdown is not a glycine deficit.
      - label: Sekhar et al. (2011)
        citation_key: sekhar_glutathione_2011
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#sekhar_glutathione_2011
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          Older adults had lower erythrocyte glutathione synthesis than younger adults, and two weeks of
          cysteine plus glycine precursor supplementation restored synthesis and concentration.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Stable-isotope erythrocyte glutathione kinetics before and after precursor supplementation.
            Cysteine was supplied as N-acetylcysteine together with glycine.
          population: Eight older adults restudied after supplementation, compared with eight younger adults.
          result: >-
            Before supplementation, older adults had lower erythrocyte glycine, cysteine, glutathione
            concentration, fractional synthesis (45.80 ± 5.69 versus 83.14 ± 6.43 %/day) and absolute
            synthesis (0.55 ± 0.12 versus 1.73 ± 0.16 mmol/L red cells per day). After two weeks, glutathione
            concentration was 94.6% higher, fractional synthesis 78.8% higher and absolute synthesis 230.9%

### Overview

Cells assemble glutathione, the main intracellular thiol, in two ATP-dependent steps. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) Glutamate–cysteine ligase joins glutamate and cysteine, then glutathione synthetase adds glycine. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) A sulfur-amino-acid-free diet slowed whole-blood synthesis in healthy young men. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) Combined precursor supplements raised erythrocyte synthesis in older adults. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) These tracer studies measured synthesis in blood cells, not in the brain. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[4]](#pm-ref-4)

- **Benefits:** Cells draw on this thiol to limit oxidative stress. In older adults, higher blood-cell synthesis after precursor supplements came with lower plasma oxidative-stress markers. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) That thiol is how sulfur amino acids from one-carbon metabolism stay connected to cellular antioxidant defence.
- **Implementation Notes:** Cysteine, methionine, glutamate, glycine, and N-acetylcysteine are the provision routes. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[4]](#pm-ref-4) A methionine-adequate cysteine-free diet did not lower erythrocyte synthesis in young men, so these results do not set a routine dose. [[5]](#pm-ref-5)
- **Biological Relevance:** Clearing peroxides and recycling oxidised glutathione are separate from this assembly. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) [[9]](#pm-ref-9)

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Glutathione formation is the point at which glutamate, cysteine and glycine become the cell's main low-molecular-weight thiol. The defining events are the two ATP-dependent assembly steps. Making the cysteine, and later using or recycling the glutathione, are separate processes.

#### (Two ATP-dependent assembly steps)

Glutathione (GSH; γ-glutamylcysteinylglycine) is built in two steps that each use ATP (the cell's energy-carrying molecule). Glutamate–cysteine ligase joins the side-chain carboxyl of glutamate to cysteine, forming γ-glutamylcysteine (a two-amino-acid intermediate) [[1]](#pm-ref-1). Glutathione synthetase then adds glycine, and the human enzyme binds one magnesium ion per subunit [[2]](#pm-ref-2). The reviewed constants for the purified first enzyme give cysteine a lower Km (0.1 mM) than glutamate (1.8 mM) [[1]](#pm-ref-1). That biochemical preference is not the same thing as a universal dietary cysteine shortage.

#### (When human blood-cell synthesis changes)

In seven healthy young men, removing methionine and cysteine from an otherwise adequate amino-acid formula for 10 days lowered whole-blood fractional synthesis from 0.65 ± 0.13 to 0.49 ± 0.13 per day and lowered absolute synthesis by about 23%, while glutathione concentration stayed near 1.2 mM. Glycine in that formula was increased, not reduced [[3]](#pm-ref-3). In older adults, erythrocyte synthesis was lower than in younger adults and rose after two weeks of a cysteine precursor, supplied as N-acetylcysteine, together with glycine [[4]](#pm-ref-4). When methionine was held at 14 mg/kg/day, cysteine intakes from zero to 40 mg/kg/day did not change erythrocyte synthesis in four young men [[5]](#pm-ref-5).

#### (What is outside the assembly reactions)

Selenium is part of glutathione peroxidase: human glutathione peroxidase uses an active-site selenocysteine and glutathione to reduce peroxides [[8]](#pm-ref-8). Riboflavin is relevant because glutathione reductase binds FAD, a riboflavin-derived cofactor, while it reduces oxidised glutathione back to the reduced form [[9]](#pm-ref-9). A dietary review groups these nutrients with glutathione support [[6]](#pm-ref-6). They act after glutathione has been made.

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

This reaction is glutathione assembly from glutamate, cysteine and glycine. Conversion of homocysteine to cysteine belongs to [BRS2-FM2-PM5 — Transsulfuration Pathway](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway). Remethylation of homocysteine belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM1](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation) and [BRS2-FM1-PM2](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation). Using glutathione to limit lipid peroxidation belongs to [BRS3-FM2-PM5 — Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control).

#### (Integration within BRS2)

Within [BRS2(FM2) — Transsulfuration & Redox Coupling](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-transsulfuration-redox-coupling), transsulfuration can supply cysteine and this reaction consumes it. Inadequacy of the shared methionine–cysteine pool can slow synthesis: whole-blood synthesis fell when both amino acids were removed [[3]](#pm-ref-3). That does not make selenium, riboflavin, or a clinical treatment part of the assembly step.

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Human tracer studies show context-dependent substrate responsiveness. Removing methionine and cysteine together reduced whole-blood glutathione synthesis, whereas removing cysteine with methionine kept adequate did not reduce erythrocyte synthesis in young men. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) In older adults with lower baseline synthesis, combined N-acetylcysteine and glycine supplementation raised erythrocyte synthesis. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) These contrasts support provision under defined conditions, not universal dietary cysteine limitation; blood-cell measurements do not establish neuronal synthesis or clinical benefit.

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS3-FM2-PM5 — Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) — Glutathione made by these assembly steps can later be consumed when peroxides are reduced. That peroxide removal, glutathione recycling, and selenium-dependent peroxidase activity are downstream of assembly.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS2-FM2-PM5 — Transsulfuration Pathway](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway) — Converts homocysteine into cysteine that the first assembly step can use. This is upstream sulfur-amino-acid supply, not the ATP-dependent reactions that form glutathione.
